clinical.vignette: This is a 60 year old female with a uterine mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: A. Perivascular epithelioid cell tumor (PEComa)

Histology: This tumor is a perivascular epithelioid cell tumor (PEComa), which is a member of a family of mesenchymal neoplasms consisting of perivascular epithelioid cells (PECs) that arise most often in the uterine corpus. Conventional PEComas consist of epithelioid or spindled cells with clear to eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. The epithelioid cells are often arranged in sheets or dyscohesive nests surrounded by thin-walled vessels. The tumor cells may exhibit permeative (tongue-like) or infiltrative growth. Other features that can be observed include a perivascular distribution of tumor cells, multinucleated cells, cells with lipid-rich or rhabdoid cytoplasm, and hyalinization of the stroma. Conventional PEComas will stain positive for melanocytic markers (HMB45, melan-A) and smooth muscle markers (SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon) with varying intensity and extent. While the majority of cases are sporadic, a subset are associated with tuberous sclerosis. Inactivating mutations of tuberous sclerosis complex 1 and 2 (TSC1/TSC2) can lead to upregulation of mTOR signaling. Thus, mTOR inhibitors may be considered a therapeutic option because of activation of mTOR signalling pathway. There are also a subset of tumors with TFE3-rearrangements or fusions, which can be confirmed by in situ hybridization. TFE3 translocation–associated PEComas would be diffusely positive for TFE3, HMB45, and cathepsin K, with focal to absent melan-A. Other tumors have RAD51B or HTR4-ST3GAL1 fusions.

Features associated with aggressive behavior in perivascular epithelioid cell tumors (PEComas) in general include size >5 cm, infiltrative growth, high nuclear grade and cellularity, mitotic index >1 MF/50 HPFs, necrosis, and vascular invasion. Tumors are classified as malignant PEComa when at least 2 of these features are present, as benign when no worrisome features are identified, and as of uncertain malignant potential when only nuclear pleomorphism or only size >5 cm is present. More specific criteria have been proposed for identifying malignant PEComas of the gynecologic tract. Based on one study, tumors with 4 or more of the following features are classified as malignant: size >5 cm, significant nuclear atypia, necrosis, lymph-vascular invasion, and mitotic index equal to or >1 MF/50 HPFs. Tumors with none of these features would be classified as benign and those with 1-3 of these features would be classified as of uncertain malignant potential. Based on a subsequent study, modified criteria for classification have been proposed. Tumors with 3 or more of the above listed features are classified as malignant and it is recommended that the remainder (those with less than 3 of those features) should be classified as of uncertain malignant potential (elimination of the benign category).

Discussion: The differential diagnosis includes endometrial stromal sarcoma (low-grade and high-grade) which usually lacks melanocytic markers. There is dispute about whether PEComas are a distinct type of neoplasm or a variant of a smooth muscle neoplasm. Recent study showed modified smooth muscle cells could represent the origin of a subset of PEComas but this observation does not dispute the recognition of PEComas as a distinct entity.

choices: Carcinosarcoma with clear cell carcinoma component

answer.text:
Answer: B. Mesonephric/mesonephric-like carcinosarcoma

Histology: This tumor is a mesonephric/mesonephric-like carcinosarcoma, which is characterized as a biphasic malignant neoplasm consisting of well-demarcated and juxtaposed epithelial (carcinomatous) and mesenchymal (sarcomatous) components. Mesonephric-like carcinosarcomas are extremely rare. The carcinomatous component consists exclusively of mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma, which displays a characteristic small tubular pattern with tubules that are lined by cuboidal epithelium with small, hyperchromatic nuclei. The epithelial component in tumors of the mesonephric type will stain positive for Pax8, CK7, GATA3, TTF and luminal CD10, but negative for WT-1, ER and PR. P53 is usually wild-type and p16 is patchy.. The mesenchymal component consists predominantly of high-grade nonspecific sarcoma, which displays elongated tumor cells with ovoid or tapered, hyperchromatic nuclei with high-grade cytologic atypia, including nuclear enlargement, pleomorphism, and brisk mitotic activity. The high-grade non-specific sarcoma component contains variable amount of cytoplasm.

Discussion: A biphasic growth pattern supports a carcinosarcoma. The carcinomatous component concerns other Mullerian-type tumor. Unlike high-grade serous carcinoma, the mesonephric-like carcinoma shows a wild-type p53 staining pattern and negative for WT-1. Most endometrioid carcinoma is positive for ER and PR. Clear cell carcinoma lacks Gata3 and TTF-1 expression.

clinical.vignette: This is 50 year old female with an ileal mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: D. Low grade endometrioid stromal sarcoma.

Histology: This tumor is a low-grade endometrioid stromal sarcoma. The malignant tumor cells resemble proliferative-phase endometrial stroma. In uterus, the tumor displays permeative or infiltrative growth (tongue-like) into the myometrium with or without lymphovascular invasion. While the tumors more commonly involve the uterine corpus, they can occur in the extrauterine location and probably arise from endometriosis. This patient had a histologically unremarkable uterus, and thus, the tumor may originate from an occult endometriosis. Microscopically, the tumor cells are arranged in irregularly, densely cellular islands. On higher power, the tumor cells have uniform, oval to fusiform nuclei with minimal to mild atypia and scant cytoplasm. Mitotic activity is usually low. There is often a delicate arteriolar network, and the tumor cells can be seen whorling around vessels. There are variant features that can be observed in this tumor including sex cord-like differentiation, fibrous/fibromyxoid changes, and smooth muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry staining will show that the tumors have strong expression of CD10, ER, and PR. Two thirds of low-grade endometrial stromal sarcomas have gene fusions involving the polycomb family genes, with the most common mutation being JAZF1-SUZ12.

Discussion: The top differential diagnosis is gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) given its location. GIST is positive for C-Kit and DOG-1, negative for ER and PR. Smooth muscle tumors, particularly leiomyosarcoma, form interlacing but disorganized fascicles. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors consist of spindle, polygonal or stellate cells growing in intersecting fascicles or set in a hypocellular (myxoid) or hyalinized background with inflammatory cells. The tumor cells are usually ALK positive.

References:

Deb PQ, Heller DS. Extrauterine endometrial stromal sarcoma: A systematic review and outcome analysis. Ann Diagn Pathol. 2022 Aug;59:151966.

clinical.vignette: This is a 20 year old female with a left ovarian mass during pregnancy. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: A. Pregnancy luteoma

Histology: This entity is a pregnancy luteoma, which is a hyperplastic diffuse, sheet-like proliferation of large, luteinized ovarian cells that occurs during pregnancy. The stroma is minimal and shows delicate blood vessels. Follicle-like spaces containing eosinophilic colloid-like secretions are commonly seen. The luteinized cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm which may contain eosinophilic globules. On higher power, the luteinized cells exhibit uniform round nuclei. Immunostains will show strong positivity of inhibin in the tumor cells. Reticulin stain will show positive fibers enclosing groups of cells, rather than individual cells. Pregnancy luteomas are a benign incidental finding near term or immediately post-partum, and they tend to regress spontaneously post-partum.

Discussion: The differential diagnosis of pregnancy luteoma can include other oxyphilic tumors of the ovary, such as luteinized thecomas and granulosa cell tumors. Luteinized thecoma would show at least focal areas of classical thecoma cells with round to oval cells containing spindled nuclei and less eosinophilic cytoplasm than seen in pregnancy luteomas. Luteinized adult granulosa cell tumor would likewise show at least focal areas of granulosa cell tumor with classical morphology. However, adult granulosa cell tumors retain evidence of sex cord architecture and do not tend to show luteinization to the extent seen in pregnancy luteomas. Steroid cell tumors can qualitatively appear histologically similar to pregnancy luteoma. Distinguishing between the two is important as a subset of steroid cell tumors are malignant. Bilaterality and a multinodular pattern favor pregnancy luteoma. In the setting of a unilateral tumor with a uninodular pattern, it may not be possible to definitively distinguish these two lesions; however, pregnancy luteoma would typically be favored based on prior odds.

clinical.vignette: This is a 40 year old female with a uterine mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: B. Fumarate hydratase-deficient atypical leiomyoma

Histology: This tumor is a fumarate hydratase (FH)-deficient atypical leiomyoma. The characteristic morphologic features include hypercellularity, eosinophilic hyaline globules, prominent staghorn vasculature, and zones of patchy alveolar pattern edema. On higher power, the tumor cells have fibrillary or neuropil-like cytoplasm, and round to ovoid nuclei with prominent macronucleoli surrounded by clear perinucleolar halos. Another histologic feature that is associated with FH deficiency is “schwannoma-like” growth with nuclear palisading. Immunohistochemical stains will show positivity for myogenic markers (desmin, SMA, caldesmon). In addition, the tumor will exhibit diffuse positive staining for 2-succinocysteine (2SC) and complete loss of staining for FH. The loss of FH IHC staining correlates with the presence of an FH gene mutation, either germline or somatic. The germline mutation in fumarate hydratase can cause hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) syndrome.

Discussion: The differential diagnosis includes perivascular epithelioid cell tumors (PEComas), which will have sheets and nests of epithelioid cells with clear to eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. They typically have thin and delicate vessels although staghorn vessels can be seen. These tumors will stain positive for melanocytic markers (HMB45, MART1), cathepsin K, and GPNMB, as well as myogenic markers (SMA, desmin, caldesmon). Leiomyosarcomas will have marked cytologic atypia with significant mitotic activity or coagulative necrosis. Classical leiomyomas have a well-demarcated border and are composed of spindle cells arranged in intersecting fascicles. The cells will have cigar-shaped nuclei with small nucleoli. Retained or variable FH staining patterns (and negative 2SC) may be observed across these other entities.

choices: Metastatic mucinous carcinoma of the lower gastrointestinal tract
Appendiceal-type low-grade mucinous neoplasm arising from a mature cystic teratoma

answer.diagnosis: Appendiceal-type low-grade mucinous neoplasm arising from a mature cystic teratoma
answer.text:
Answer: C. Appendiceal-type low-grade mucinous neoplasm arising from a mature cystic teratoma.

Histology: This tumor is an appendiceal-type low-grade mucinous neoplasm arising from a mature cystic teratoma. The tumor is composed of cysts lined by one or two layers of columnar mucinous cells contiguous or noncontiguous with other teratomatous elements. The epithelium is hypermucinous and goblet-cell rich, exhibiting morphologic features of gastrointestinal-type mucinous differentiation identical to the morphology of appendiceal origin. Extracellular mucin is present within ovarian stroma as pools or dissecting lakes, representing the presence of pseudomyxoma ovarii. The teratomatous elements may or may not contain more than one germ layer, including ectodermal elements (squamous epithelium and cutaneous adnexal structures) found in a dermoid cyst. Other tissues that can be found in teratomas include neuroectodermal derivatives (glial tissue, ependyma, and cerebellum, neuronal tissue), mesodermal derivatives (adipose tissue, bone, cartilage, smooth muscle), and endodermal derivatives (respiratory epithelium, thyroid, salivary gland, gastrointestinal), among many others. Mucinous tumors in general are present in 2-11% of ovarian mature cystic teratomas. Teratoma-associated mucinous tumors can range in appearance from cystadenomatous or borderline tumor-like to adenocarcinoma. These tumors share morphologic and immunohistochemical features of low-grade mucinous tumors of appendiceal origin, often displaying a CK7 negative, CK20 positive immunoprofile.

Discussion: Metastatic mucinous carcinoma of the lower gastrointestinal tract to the ovary is certainly on the differential diagnosis. However, in this case, the appendix was entirely examined microscopically and showed no evidence of tumor. Other characteristic features of metastatic disease would include bilateral ovarian tumor, nodularity with surface involvement, and extraovarian tumor morphologically similar to the primary tumor. Mucinous borderline tumors would contain cysts lined by proliferative mucinous epithelium forming tufts and have cystic growth displaying greater degrees of architectural complexity and epithelial stratification. These tumors would exhibit CK7-positive and CK20-negative immunoprofiles. Mucinous cystadenomas are composed of cysts lined by 1 or 2 layers of columnar mucinous cells with minor foci exhibiting focal epithelial budding and branching. These tumors also exhibit CK7-positive and CK20-negative immunoprofiles.

answer.diagnosis: Uterine tumor resembling ovarian sex cord tumor (UTROSCT)
answer.text:
Answer: D. Uterine Tumor Resembling Ovarian Sex Cord Tumor (UTROSCT)

Histology: This entity is a uterine tumor resembling ovarian sex cord tumor (UTROSCT). The tumor in this case has an infiltrating type pattern with cord-like architecture and cytology that can be seen in the ovary but is located in the uterus. Small tubular glands are present resembling those observed in Sertoli cell tumors, which are sex-cord stromal tumors in the ovary. These tumors can also display a wide morphologic spectrum, including solid and corded patterns, pushing bordeers or infiltrating type patterns, retiform pattern, tubular pattern, and lipidized tumor cells. The tumor cells are small and epithelioid with round to oval nuclei and minimal mitotic activity. Along with characteristic morphology resembling sex cord stromal tumors, another feature is a polyphenotypic immunoprofile. Immunohistochemistry can show positive expression of cytokeratin (panCK), smooth muscle markers (desmin), endometrial stromal markers, and sex cord markers (inhibin, SF1, calretinin). If a fusion panel is performed, these tumors often have fusions involving NCOA1/2/3 and ESR1. Features suggesting malignant potential have been proposed.

Discussion: The differential diagnosis includes smooth muscle tumors such as leiomyomas and leiomyosarcomas, particularly those with collageneous stroma and hydropic change, which are features that can impart an epithelial-like appearance. However, UTROSCTs typically do not display hydropic change. Epithelioid smooth muscle tumors may also enter in the differential diagnosis based on their morphologic appearance and immunohistochemical profile. Low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma can have an infiltrative type pattern and sex cord differentiation to a minor degree, but no pronounced epithelial-type pattern. Moreover, low grade endometrial stromal sarcomas have different genetic profiles (JAZF1 or PHF1 fusions, etc.).

clinical.vignette: This is a 60 yo female who had a hysterectomy after an endometrial biopsy diagnosis. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Endometrial endometrioid carcinoma with extensive squamous differentiation
HPV-associated primary cervical squamous cell carcinoma

answer.text:
Answer: C. Primary endometrial squamous cell carcinoma

Histology: This tumor is a primary endometrial squamous cell carcinoma. The endometrium is replaced by nests of well-differentiated keratinizing squamous proliferations that have an exophytic papillary growth pattern, a broad pushing border, and small foci of irregular nests and single cells that invade myometrium. The tumor contains pink necrotic areas, keratin pearl formation, and dyskeratosis. The tumor cells have rare mitotic activity, including atypical forms. The entire cervix was submitted and showed no involvement of squamous cell carcinoma. There was no malignant glandular component within the endometrium. However, there were benign endometrial and endocervical glands at the endomyometrial interface. Altogether, these findings characterize a primary endometrial squamous cell carcinoma, which is a diagnosis of exclusion. This tumor is rare and represents <1% of all endometrial tumors. Endometrial squamous cell carcinomas show aberrant/mutation-type p53 expression, are negative for ER, PR, and p16, and have no detectable HPV by ISH. Per whole-exome sequencing, these tumors can have co-mutations in TP53 and CDKN2A.

Discussion: Endometrial endometrioid carcinoma with squamous differentiation (EECSD) contains a coexisting endometrial adenocarcinoma. The presence of a glandular component of the tumor and primary site of the disease located in the uterine corpus would suggest this entity. Thus, the endometrium should be entirely submitted to rule out an EECSD. EECSD would have immature squamous type differentiation and would not be cytologically malignant. Whereas, this tumor is a keratinizing well-differentiated type squamous lesion. Primary cervical squamous cell carcinoma extending to the endometrium should be excluded by submitting the entire cervix. An HPV-associated cervical squamous cell carcinoma will have diffuse or block positive immunohistochemical staining of p16 or ISH detection of HPV, unlike this entity that is HPV and p16 negative. A metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma would have a primary site of disease located in the skin and should have a distribution of disease in the uterine corpus that is not endometrial-based.

clinical.vignette: This is a 30 yo female with a hysterectomy performed for a presumed leiomyoma. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: A. Low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma

Histology: This is a low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma. This malignant stromal tumor has a tongue-like pattern of infiltration through the myometrium with or without lymphovascular invasion. The tumor cells may whorl around small arteriolar-type vessels throughout the whole tumor, reminiscent of proliferative phase endometrial stroma. The neoplastic cells are spindle to oval with small, round, uniform nuclei and have no significant atypia or mitotic activity. Necrosis, foamy histiocytes, hyaline-type deposits, or cystic change can be seen. These tumors may stain positive for CD10, IFITM1, WT1, ER, PR, keratins, smooth muscle markers (desmin and h-caldesmon), sex cord markers (inhibin, calretinin, melan-A, CD99), and beta catenin. However, they typically have CD10 overexpression with very little muscle marker expression except for cases with smooth muscle differentiation. In terms of genetics, low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma can frequently contain fusions, such as JAZF1/JJAZ1.

Discussion: The differential diagnosis includes leiomyosarcomas, which contain large thick-walled blood vessels with fascicular architecture, but the tumor cells show spindle cell differentiation and contain marked cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and necrosis. High-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma has more atypia and mitotic activity than that seen in low-grade tumors. High-grade endometrial stromal sarcomas also have YWHAE-NUTM2AB/fusions, BCOR fusions, or internal tandem duplications; they are frequently positive for Cyclin D1 and BCOR while negative for ER/PR, which contrasts with low-grade endometrial stromal sarcomas that are positive for ER/PR, but negative for BCOR and Cyclin D1. Endometrial stromal nodule is a benign counterpart with the same cytology as low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma but has a circumscribed interface between myometrium and stroma with absent to minimal myometrial invasion. This differs from the pattern of infiltration seen in endometrial stromal sarcomas. Interestingly, endometrial stromal nodules may contain the same fusions seen in low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma, which suggests that the two are related through the same pathogenesis pathway.

answer.diagnosis: Sertoli-leydig cell tumor with high-grade sarcomatous component
answer.text:
Answer: A. Sertoli-leydig cell tumor with high-grade sarcomatous component

Histology: This tumor is a moderately-poorly differentiated sertoli-leydig cell tumor with high-grade sarcomatous component. The tumor focally has a lobular pattern containing sertoli cells growing as nests or solid tubules or cords with moderate cytologic atypia and conspicuous mitotic activity. At the periphery of the lobules are leydig cells with eosinophilic, plump cytoplasm present in clusters. There is also sarcomatoid stroma resembling primitive gonadal stroma. Heterologous elements can be observed in approximately 20% of these tumors and be epithelial or mesenchymal. In this case, this tumor contains heterologous elements with sarcomatous transformation to rhabdomyosarcoma as demonstrated by primitive-looking skeletal muscle. The sertoli cells and leydig cells will stain positive for sex cord markers (α-inhibin, calretinin, SF1, WT1, and FOXL2). The rhabdomyosarcoma will stain positive for myogenin. While moderately and poorly differentiated tumors behave in a malignant fashion, the presence of heterologous skeletal muscle as an additional poor prognostic feature. These tumors are mostly sporadic, but can occur in DICER1 syndrome.

Discussion: Since a rhabdomyosarcoma component is present, the top differential is a carcinosarcoma. However, the other component is a sex-cord stromal tumor rather than a carcinoma. Likewise, the presence of moderately to poorly differentiated sertoli-leydig cell tumor argues against undifferentiated carcinoma or adenosarcoma with rhabdomyosarcomatous overgrowth.

answer.text:
Answer: D. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of ovary

Histology: This benign and rare tumor is a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm typically confined to the ovary and resembling its pancreatic counterpart. These tumors show an admixture of three primary histologic patterns: solid, nests, and pseudopapillae. In this case, the solid component is punctuated by cysts. Nests of cells are separated by hyalinized stroma and the pseudopapillae appear to have hyalinized cores. There are frequent intracytoplasmic and extracytoplasmic eosinophilic hyaline globules. On higher power, the cytology shows polygonal cells with eosinophilic to pale and foamy cytoplasm with paranuclear vacuoles. The nuclei are cytologically bland, round, with grooves, exhibiting minimal atypia and no mitotic activity. The tumor cells are positive for CD10, CD56, CD99, WT1, β-catenin (nuclear and cytoplasmic), and α1-antitrypsin, and they may stain for CAM5.2 (dot-like perinuclear), PR, synaptophysin, and KIT (CD117). Most tumor contain CTNNB1 mutations.

Discussion: Both solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of ovary and microcystic stromal tumor have CTNNB1 mutations, however, the latter lacks a pseudopapillary growth pattern or the characteristic nuclear grooves of solid pseudopapillary tumor. Adult granulosa cell tumor (AGCT) usually exhibits nuclear grooves but lacks abundant eosinophilic globules. In yolk sac tumor, eosinophilic hyaline globules may be conspicuous both within cells and in the stroma, but this tumor expresses germ cell markers.

clinical.vignette: This is a 40 year old female with a right ovarian mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: B. Microcystic stromal tumor

Histology: This ovarian mass is a microcystic stromal tumor. A majority of these stromal tumors exhibit the classic triad of microcysts, solid cellular zones, and fibrous stroma, in various proportions. On low power, the microcystic areas as well as solid cellular areas are intersected by fibrous stroma with hyaline plaques. The microcysts consist of small to large-sized oval to round cystic spaces, in areas merging into larger irregular channels. Rarely, there are variants of microcystic stromal tumors that are predominantly or entirely composed of diffuse, corded, or nested cells with absence of apparent microcysts. On high power, the tumor cells contain a moderate amount of finely granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles can be identified. The nuclei are bland, round to oval with small indistinct nucleoli and a low mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry staining of the tumor cells will be positive for nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin, and positive for CD10, WT1, FOXL2, cyclin D1, and SF1, but negative for inhibin, calretinin, and EMA. Most microcystic stromal tumors have a point mutation in CTNNB1 (encoding β-catenin) or mutation in APC. These tumors can be associated with familial adenomatous polyposis.

Discussion: Microcystic stromal tumor has overlapping features with other sex-cord stromal tumor including adult granulosa cell tumor, fibrothecoma and steroid cell tumor. However, its distinct immuoprofile can facilitate the classification. Morphologically, even in the solid variant, focal microcysts can be seen.

clinical.vignette: This is a 30 year old female with an abdominal wall mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: D. Metastatic epithelioid trophoblastic tumor

Histology: This is an epithelioid trophoblastic tumor that has metastasized to the abdominal wall. Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor is a malignant neoplasm of chorionic-type intermediate trophoblast. This tumor is characterized by nests or cords of round, plump, uniform cells in a fibrous sclerotic stroma with fat intermixed. There are tumor cell islands centered around vessels in a perivascular distribution. There is also notable geographic necrosis and eosinophilic hyaline-like material present in the center of tumor nests or between tumor cells. On higher power, the tumor cells have moderate amount of finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, distinct cell membranes, round nuclei, and small prominent nucleoli. The mitotic count will vary. The tumor cells will stain positive for HSD3B1, HLA-G, p63, cyclin E, α-inhibin, and GATA3. In some cases, a Ki-67 proliferation index of >10% is helpful for diagnosis. This patient had a past medical history of epithelioid trophoblastic tumor, consistent with the diagnosis. There is a mild to moderate elevation of serum hCG of <2500 mIU/mL that can be detected in 80% of cases. Metastasis can occur in 25-30% of cases.

Discussion: The differential diagnosis includes choriocarcinoma, which is another type of gestational trophoblastic disease. However, choriocarcinoma consists of three different cell types (syncytial trophoblastic cells and cytotrophoblastic cells as well as intermediate trophoblast cells) that are cells that normally form part of the placenta. Placental site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT) is also a neoplastic proliferation of implantation-type intermediate trophoblast, however, the tumor will be positive for HPL and negative for p63 negative. This contrasts with the HPL negativity and p63 positivity seen in epithelioid trophoblastic tumors. Squamous cell carcinoma is on the differential, however, it usually does not have an increase in hCG, is negative for trophoblastic differentiation markers, and has definitive cell bridges and true keratin formation, unlike epithelioid trophoblastic tumors.

clinical.vignette: This is a 60 year old female with a left ovarian mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Answer: D. Sertoli-leydig cell tumor

Histology: This is a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, composed of varying proportions of Sertoli and Leydig cells intersected by fibrous or edematous connective tissue. The sertoliform tubules are bland and immature-looking and arranged in nests or cords. These Sertoli cells have poorly defined cell borders, scant cytoplasm, and small oval to round nuclei. Between the sertoliform tubules are clusters of Leydig cells, which contain abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Subtypes of Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors according to the criteria of the World Health Organization (WHO) include well-differentiated, moderately differentiated, poorly differentiated, and retiform. This case is a well-differentiated tumor, which contains Sertoli cells arranged in a tubular pattern separated by more Leydig cells and has no DICER1 mutation. The cells lining the tubules exhibit little nuclear atypia and only rare mitotic figures. However, it is more common for these tumors to be moderately or poorly differentiated. Moderately differentiated tumors consist of immature cords or islands of Sertoli cells. Well-defined tubules may be present with mature Leydig cells. Poorly differentiated tumors have sheet-like growth of spindle-shaped tumor cells resembling sarcomas. These tumors may lose immature cords of cells and exhibit cellular atypia with more mitoses. The periphery of moderately to poorly differentiated tumors may contain heterologous elements, such as skeletal muscle, cartilage, and mucinous glands. Irregular slit-like spaces and retiform patterns can be present. These moderately and poorly differentiated tumors are mostly sporadic but can occur in DICER1 syndrome.

Discussion: The differential diagnosis of sertoli-leydig cell tumor depends on their degree of differentiation and presence of heterologous or retiform components. Well-differentiated tumors may be confused with well-differentiated sertoliform endometrioid carcinoma as the glands and solid epithelial formations in this latter tumor might resemble the hollow and solid tubules of sertoli-leydig cell tumors. However, endometrioid carcinoma will have areas with the usual pattern of endometrioid caricnoma and presence of mucin at the apical borders of the tumor cells. CK7/EMA will stain positively, while inhibin and SF-1 will stain negatively in endometrioid carcinoma. Whereas, the converse is true for sertoli-leydig cell tumors. Granulosa cell tumor may have small foci of tubules indistinguishable from sertoli-leydig cell tumors. However, granulosa cells tend to be mature with pale, often grooved nuclei whereas Sertoli cells are commonly immature. Moreover, the presence of heterologous elements would never be encountered in granulosa cell tumors and is specific for sertoli-leydig cell tumors. Sertoli-cell tumors are solid with fibromatous stroma and lack leydig cell components seen here.

clinical.vignette: This is a 30 year old female with a right ovarian mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: C. Seromucinous borderline tumor

Histology: This is a seromucinous borderline tumor, which is characterized by papillae with hierarchical branching as seen in serous tumors and mucinous cells resembling those in the endocervix. Larger papillae consist of edematous or fibrous stroma filled with acute inflammatory cells, such as neutrophils. There is absence of stromal invasion and absence of micropapillary architecture measuring >5mm, consistent with the classification as a borderline tumor. The epithelial lining of the papillae is often tufted, stratified, and cytologically bland. The glands are lined by mucinous epithelium with basal nuclei and abundant apical cytoplasm, resembling the epithelium of the endocervix. Multiple Mullerian cell types (endocervical-type mucinous cells, ciliated cells, hobnail cells, and eosinophilic cells) are admixed in the epithelium in different proportions. The epithelial cells are typically positive for CK7, PAX8, ER, and PR, and negative for WT1, CK20, and CDX2. Approximately 30% of these tumors are bilateral. These tumors have an association with endometriosis, most commonly endometriotic cysts. Other tumors that are associated with endometriosis include endometrioid carcinoma and clear cell carcinoma.

Discussion: Seromucinous borderline tumors have papillary architecture closely resembling serous tumors but contain endocervical-type mucinous epithelium, which is negative for WT-1. In contrast, serous borderline tumors consist of epithelial cells that are low cuboidal with not much-rich cytoplasm, and the epithelial cells would be positive for WT1. Mucinous borderline tumors would display glandular and cystic architecture rather than predominantly papillary architecture (although mucinous borderline tumors can have villous architecture), and the predominant cell-type has intestinal-type mucinous cytoplasm with presence of goblet cells or Paneth cells. Seromucinous carcinoma (considered to be variants of endometrioid carcinoma with mucinous diffferentiation in the current WHO Classification) would have more cytologic atypia and architectural complexity than seromucinous borderline tumors. Furthermore, seromucinous carcinomas may exhibit a complex cribriform growth pattern involving the surface of papillae or lining cystic spaces.

clinical.vignette: This is a 45-year-old female with a large renal mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Angiomyolipoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a predominantly bland adipocytic proliferation lined by wispy fibrous septae with varying amounts of chronic inflammation. Fibrinoid, proteinaceous areas are present within the septae; however, they lack the appearance of hyalinized, eosinophilic features that are characteristic of fibrin thrombi . Stains for melanocytic differentiation were positive (HMB45 and MelanA), thereby confirming the diagnosis of angiomyolipoma (AML)

Discussion:

Angiomyolipoma (AML) is a member of the PEComa family of tumors (perivascular epithelioid cell tumor family), and despite their name, may have an uneven/varying proportion of angiomatoid, smooth muscle/myoid, and lipomatous components. They are presumed to arise from a perivascular epithelioid cell, which has no known normal human counterpart. In some cases, one component may be predominant, and careful consideration of the location (the kidneys being a common site for this tumor) and the patient's age/sex (F>M, 4th to 5th decades) hints at the diagnosis of AML. They are usually discovered sporadically, and commonly contain mutations in TSC2 or TSC1 with loss of heterozygosity of chromosome 16p and/or loss of 5q.

The distribution of staining for HMB45 and MelanA in AML is peculiar. HMB45 stains 90% of the adipose tissue, 85% of the myoid component, and 80% of the vasculature, while MelanA stains, to a lesser degree, 70% of the adipose component, 60% of the smooth muscle component, and 40% of the vasculature. Cathepsin K is also a useful marker for distinguishing AMLs.

Lipomas would display mature adipocytic differentiation but are not expected to be positive for HMB45 and MelanA, and the kidney/perirenal space would not be a common site for lipoma. A myelolipoma most commonly arises in the adrenal gland and is characterized by a tumor with juxtaposition of mature fatty tissue and hematopoietic elements. Angiolipoma would demonstrate greater stromal vasculature and fibrin thrombi are characteristic.

Angiomyolipomas may assume an epithelioid cytologic configuration and may appear pleomorphic, and is important to recognize as the epithelioid variant has metastatic potential. Epithelioid AMLs may demonstrate p53 mutations. A potential pitfall with the differential of well-differentiated liposarcoma is that some fat predominant AMLs may rarely demonstrate MDM2 amplification.

clinical.vignette: This is a 76-year-old male with a pancreatic cyst. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia with chronic pancreatitis
Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) with background chronic pancreatitis

answer.diagnosis: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) with background chronic pancreatitis
answer.text:
Correct answer: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) with background chronic pancreatitis

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of pancreas with a large dominating cyst lined by mucinous epithelium with vague papillary infoldings, along with several other cysts that demonstrate a similar architectural pattern. The background lobulated pancreas appears atrophic and inflamed, yet the lobules maintain their configuration and the cells do not display 4:1 nuclear ratio abnormalities. These findings are consistent with an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) with background chronic pancreatitis. This case was positive for MUC5, confirming the diagnosis.

Discussion:

IPMN is a cystic pancreatic neoplasm, usually in the head, that is known for its association with invasive carcinoma. They are subtyped into gastric, intestinal, and pancreatobiliary types based on the epithelial lining and contents (gastric type mucosa, intestinal mucosa, or biliary-type epithelium), as well as oncocytic-type (IOPMN). IPMNs may be further divided into low-grade and high-grade dysplasia. It is most prevalent in men in the 7th to 8th decades and incidence has been rising due to enhanced detection via CT scan and MRI.

Pancreatic cyst fluid analysis with ancillary molecular studies may assist in determining what type of cyst (serous, mucinous) especially if there is elevated cyst fluid CEA and GNAS mutations that may point towards a mucinous cyst.

Morphologically, IPMNs are characterized by cystic spaces with papillary projections lined by gastric-type (cells resembling gastric foveolae and sometimes with intestinal metaplasia), intestinal type (tall columnar epithelium that resembles intestinal villous adenomas), and pancreatobiliary type (complex, thin branching papillae with biliary-appearing glands and low cuboidal cells with prominent nucleoli). Based on the histologic findings in the current case, this may be best classified as a gastric type IPMN without high-grade dysplasia, as the lining resembles gastric foveolae and there are no atypical mitoses nor hyperchromasia.

The background pancreas may have been obstructed due to the compression from the cystic IPMN, leading to pancreatic secretion backup and eventual lobular atrophy that is evidenced here as background chronic pancreatitis. The slit-like glands in the lobules and the increased chronic inflammation may be confused for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma; however, there is no stark variation in nuclear size (4:1 nuclear size discrepancy between adjacent glands), and the glands retain a lobular configuration.

Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) is defined as a nontumoral form of dysplasia and would not have clinical, mass-forming manifestations (i.e., they are defined as microscopic incidental findings). They commonly arise next to areas of invasive carcinoma. The clinical history of a cystic pancreatic mass with gastric foveolar epithelium should point one to a diagnosis of IPMN instead of PanIN, and since gastric type IPMNs have significant morphologic overlap with PanIN, obtaining adequate clinical history of a cystic pancreatic mass is critical to the diagnosis of IPMN.

clinical.vignette: This is a 60-year-old male with a pancreatic mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreas

answer.text:
Correct answer: Pancreatoblastoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a well-circumscribed, encapsulated solid lesion with amphophilic cells separated by wispy fibrous septae; these display acinar differentiation. In areas, the cells take on a more eosinophilic appearance with exuberant cytoplasm, and some areas show squamoid whorling. The nuclei exhibit clearing, vesiculated chromatin, and some prominent nucleoli. The combination of squamoid whorls and solid growth with acinar differentiation is diagnostic of pancreatoblastoma.

Discussion:

Pancreatoblastoma is commonly thought to involve children under the age of 10 years; however, it can rarely present in adults and has been shown to be equally aggressive in older individuals. It is characterized by a sheet-like proliferation of neoplastic cells that display at least 2 lines of differentiation common to the pancreas: acinar, ductal, and/or neuroendocrine. The presence of squamoid nests is a characteristic diagnostic feature. These tumors have a proclivity for the pancreatic head, and are associated with both Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (which also leads to increased risk for Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma and hepatoblastoma) and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). In children, CEA and AFP may be useful preoperative diagnostic tests, but they are less tightly correlated in adults. Pancreatoblastoma, most notably, would display nuclear beta-catenin staining in the squamoid nests. Cytokeratin, acinar markers (e.g. trypsin), ductal markers (e.g. CEA, CK19), and neuroendocrine markers if present (e.g. synaptophysin) would be positive.

Acinar cell carcinoma would not show squamoid nests or other lineages, and thus would not have nuclear beta-catenin staining. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma would exhibit greater nuclear atypia, have no squamoid nests, and would be positive for neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1). Lastly, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN) would not demonstrate acinar differentiation nor squamoid nests and instead display pseudopapillary structures with neoplastic cells falling off of fibrovascular cores. SPN would be diffusely positive for nuclear beta-catenin, unlike in pancreatoblastoma.

clinical.vignette: This is a 40-year-old female with a mandibular mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of nests, cords, and sheets of polygonal, eosinophilic, squamoid cells with ample cytoplasm and pleomorphic nuclei in an admixed background of grungy to psammomatous calcification and amyloid-like matrix. The combination of these polygonal cells, the grungy calcification, and the amyloid-like matrix deposition is suggestive of the diagnosis of calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor.

Discussion:

Calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor (CEOT), also formerly known as Pindborg tumor (after the Danish pathologist Jens Pindborg who discovered the entity in 1955) is a rare, benign neoplasm usually of the premolar and molar mandibular regions (posterior mandible). A subset of cases may also be identified in the maxilla or in the gingiva, where it is known as a peripheral tumor. About 50% of cases of CEOT are associated with an unerupted or impacted tooth. Radiologically they resemble a dentigerous cyst with lesions demonstrating lucency with varying degrees of scattered calcifications (from lucent to dense), giving a “driven snow” appearance on radiography. Histologically, CEOT is characterized by the combination of pleomorphic polyhedral squamous epithelial cells with intercellular bridging, focal psammomatous bodies, amyloid bodies comprised of degenerated keratin filaments, and basophilic calcifications and a lack of architectural pleomorphism (no whorls, or cribriform pattern). The clear cell variant may demonstrate clear, vacuolated cytoplasm. The amyloid component may react with Congo red stain.

The lesion occurs in patients of the 4th to 5th decade and may be invasive and exhibit local recurrence status post resection, but prognostically it is less aggressive than ameloblastoma.

Ademonatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) usually occurs in females below the age of 20 years with a propensity for an impacted tooth in the anterior maxilla. Histologically it would demonstrate nodular, squamoid islands and cribriform architecture surrounded by a thick fibrous capsule. Adenoid ameloblastoma can also be associated with impacted teeth, but histologically they demonstrate extensive dentinoid clear cells with occasional ghost cells arranged in morules and whorls like AOT that is not typical of CEOT. Lastly, dentigerous cysts are another entity associated with unerupted teeth, but radiographically are fluid-filled lesions that encase the crown of the unerupted tooth of individuals in the 3rd and 4th decades. Histologically it is composed of inflamed stratified squamous epithelium without basal palisading.

clinical.vignette: This is a 50-year-old male with a nasal mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of pieces of tumor with exuberant chronic inflammation and areas of cribriform glands and squamous pearl formation, with scattered areas demonstrating basaloid morphology. This case was positive upon HPV in-situ-hybridization immunohistochemistry. The IHC findings and the combined presence of cribriform glands and squamous differentiation points to a diagnosis of HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma.

Discussion:

HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma is a neoplasm described as recently as 2013 that is located exclusively in the sinonasal tract and is noted for its strong association with human papillomavirus 33 (HPV33) and its negativity for MYB/NFIB translocations. This tumor was formerly known as HPV-related sinonasal carcinoma with adenoid cystic carcinoma-like features. It is noted for its wide age range, and high risk HPV is detected in all reported cases, with HPV 33 detected in 68% [Head Neck Pathol 2018 Sep 26]. The usual histologic features include areas that resemble ACC with tubular, cribriform, and solid patterns, as evidenced by biphasic ductal and myoepithelial differentiation, as well as squamous and basaloid differentiation. Rarely, sarcomatoid areas with staghorn vasculature or heterologous mesenchymal elements may be present.

Based on the curated cases in the literature, this neoplasm is associated with high frequency of late local recurrence decades after initial surgery but distant metastases are rare. Current treatment revolves around surgical resection with negative margins and sometimes radiation therapy.

Though ACC shares morphologic overlap with HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma, ACC would not be positive for high-risk HPV in-situ hybridization and has no known association with HPV infection. ACC would also have a MYB/NFIB translocation in most cases. Sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma would be characterized by predominantly squamous differentiation and no biphasic morphology nor myoepithelial differentiation. Lastly, SMARCB1 deficient sinonasal carcinoma would demonstrate INI1/BAF47 (SMARCB1) loss by immunohistochemistry, and it will be HPV-ISH negative.

clinical.vignette: This is a 75-year-old male with a hard palate mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Polymorphous adenocarcinoma

Histology:

Histologic sections demonstrate an infiltrative mass arranged in cohesive lobules with faint myxoid areas and separating bands of sclerotic collagen the lobules contain a variety of patterns ranging from cribriform-like to nested to sheet-like. Upon further inspection of the cytologic features, the cells appear to be of a single type, the nuclei appear mostly uniform, and there are few mitotic figures and no atypical mitoses. The cytologic uniformity, architectural complexity, and the characteristic palate location are in keeping with the diagnosis of polymorphous adenocarcinoma.

Discussion:

Polymorphous adenocarcinoma (PLGA) characteristically occurs in the palate of females in the sixth to seventh decades, although it may also occur in the minor, and rarely major salivary glands over a wide age range. This carcinoma usually exhibits indolent behavior and is characterized by uniform cytologic features with diverse architectural patterns, most notably cribriform-like, solid, trabecular, and nested patterns. A characteristic growth pattern of PLGA involves columns and rows of single cells infiltrating adjacent tissues/salivary gland and extending to the overlying epithelium, if present. Of note cribriform adenocarcinoma of the salivary gland, a variant of polymorphous adenocarcinoma where cribriform pattern is dominant, is associated with more aggressive behavior and a higher frequency of lymph node metastasis.

It had been postulated in studies by Batsakis, Freedman et al in the early 1980s that this neoplasm may be derived from the terminal duct of the salivary gland lobule.

PLGA is characterized by molecular alterations in the PRKD gene, most notably in the PRKD1 E710D hotspot.

ACC is a biphasic, aggressive salivary gland neoplasm demonstrating ductal and myoepithelial cell differentiation, commonly with a cribriform to solid architectural pattern. It is typically p63/p40 (+) as opposed to PLGA, which is p63+/p40-. In essence, absence of p40 staining in PLGA, which is a more sensitive marker of myoepithelial differentiation, reveals that PLGAs do not harbor myoepithelial elements and also highlights ACC's biphasic morphology. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is an encapsulated neoplasm with mucous, intermediate, and epidermoid cell elements interspersed with columnar, clear cell, or oncocytic features and arranged in a solid, cystic, and sometimes papillary or glandular growth pattern. Lastly, cellular pleomorphic adenoma (PA) may, as the name implies, exhibit increased cellularity compared to a conventional PA (with ductal, myoepithelial, and myxoid stromal elements); identification of chondromyxoid stroma is key in the diagnosis.

clinical.vignette: This is an adult female with a skin nodule. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Invasive lobular carcinoma and seborrheic keratosis

answer.diagnosis: Invasive lobular carcinoma and seborrheic keratosis
answer.text:
Correct answer: Invasive lobular carcinoma and seborrheic keratosis.

Histology:

Histologic sections are comprised of pseudohorn cysts and epithelial hyperplasia at the surface of the nodule, which are reminiscent of seborrheic keratosis (SK). However, deeper to the SK, there is a hyperchromatic, invasive linear cell population that percolates through collagen bundles into the subcutaneous fat. The nuclei appear plasmacytoid and the cells have amphophilic cytoplasm. The patient had a history of breast cancer, and the findings are most consistent with an invasive lobular carcinoma involving a seborrheic keratosis.

Discussion:

Invasive lobular carcinoma may be extremely bland on low power, and thus recognition of patient history, as well as an immunohistochemical workup using cytokeratins and hormonal markers (estrogen receptor and/or progesterone receptor) may be useful. On medium to high magnification the cells appear to percolate in linear formation like a "soldier's march", and the cells may be discohesive and plasmacytoid.

Melanoma, especially the desmoplastic subtype, may be subtle on low power just like invasive lobular carcinoma; however, desmoplastic melanoma subtype stains for Sox10 and S100 and, interestingly, is negative for MelanA and HMB45. This is suggestive of the theory that desmoplastic melanoma is a subtype that shows differentiation towards a more neural-tissue-like phenotype. Other subtypes of melanoma (lentigo maligna, among others) will be positive for not only Sox10 and S100 but HMB45 and MelanA.

Gastrointestinal signet ring cell carcinoma may be notoriously difficult to detect, and the index of suspicion for a metastatic signet ring cell carcinoma is high in a patient with this cancer as their known primary. To make matters complicated, some forms of invasive lobular carcinoma may demonstrate a signet ring-like morphology. Immunohistochemical stains that may be useful include CDX2 to rule in signet ring cell carcinoma, and ER, PR, GATA3, and mammaglobin to rule out invasive lobular carcinoma.

clinical.vignette: This is an adult female with an 11 cm breast mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Metaplastic carcinoma with lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)

answer.diagnosis: Metaplastic carcinoma with lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)
answer.text:
Correct answer: Metaplastic carcinoma with lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)

Histology:

Histologic sections are comprised of a hypercellular, infiltrative lesion with rampant mitotic activity and atypical mitoses, marked cytologic atypia with large epithelioid to spindled cells with crinkled nuclear contours and vesicular chromatin, and gland formation. Adjacent to the bulk of the lesion is an area of lobular filling, which imparts a vacuolated appearance between each lobular cell. This adjacent finding is indicative of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), and the main mass lesion is a metaplastic carcinoma arising in association with LCIS.

Discussion:

Metaplastic carcinoma (MC) is a varied, heterogenous group of triple negative (ER-, PR-, HER2-) invasive breast cancers that characteristically demonstrate differentiation of the neoplastic epithelial elements (in this case, may stem from the LCIS) into squamous cells or mesenchymal-appearing cells. The mesenchymal cells may be chondroid, spindled, or osseous, among others. Essentially, an invasive breast carcinoma or precursor lesion accompanied by a squamoid, spindled, or mesenchymal element is necessary for the diagnosis, and cases that lack an in situ or invasive component require a immunohistochemical panel to look for evidence of epithelial differentiation (i.e., HMWCK, p63, p40). Of note, the term sarcomatoid carcinoma of the breast is no longer favored.

Metaplastic carcinoma, as a group, encompasses aggressive lesions; however, fibromatosis-like MC and low-grade adenosquamous carcinomas are usually more indolent and have a better prognosis. Thus, given the glandular formations in this case it is important to determine if a gland-producing lesion in a squamoid to spindled background may, in fact, be adenosquamous carcinoma. In our case, the frequent mitoses, spindle cell atypia, absence of lymphoid aggregates, and the atypia of the epithelial component instead favor a metaplastic carcinoma.

Molecularly, metaplastic carcinomas have been shown to involve downregulation of the CCN6 pathway and Wnt gene mutations.

Phyllodes tumor would usually present with a neoplastic stromal component with benign epithelial elements, unlike the areas of LCIS seen here. It would usually be keratin/p63/p40 negative; however, a subset of cases show immunopositivity for keratins and squamous markers which is a diagnostic pitfall. CD34 should be positive in phyllodes tumor and negative in metaplastic carcinoma.

Adenomyoepithelioma is a well-circumscribed, lobulated, benign biphasic tumor of epithelial and myoepithelial cells, with spindle cell, tubular, and lobulated variants. The myoepithelial cells can be highlighted via immunohistochemistry with calponin/smooth muscle myosin heavy chain (SMMHC) or p63 as surrounding the epithelial elements. Significant nuclear atypia or mitoses would not be typical of adenomyoepithelioma.

clinical.vignette: This is a teenage female with a 7 cm breast mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Histology:

Histologic sections are comprised of a leaf-like, arborizing proliferation of eosinophilic spindled cells in an exaggerated intracanalicular pattern. The proliferation of spindled cells takes up an entire 4x magnification field of view. There is mild variation in stromal cellularity, with hypercellular areas merging into more hypocellular areas. Some areas contain stromal giant cells and other areas contain bland epithelial elements. Peripheral stromal condensation and subepithelial stromal condensation are present. Taken together these findings raise concern for malignant phyllodes tumor.

Discussion:

Phyllodes tumor is a biphasic, fibroepithelial lesion that demonstrates aberrant epithelial-to-stromal interaction that is believed to be involved in phyllodes tumorigenesis. The loss of epithelial interactions in the stromal component are what is thought to lead to malignant progression. The grading of phyllodes tumors spans the categories of benign, borderline, and malignant. Of note, the mere presence of malignant heterologous elements (chondroid, osteosarcomatoid, among others) directly upgrades to the malignant phyllodes tumor category.

Benign phyllodes tumors tend to have mild stromal atypia, mildly increased stromal cellularity, and absent stromal overgrowth (overgrowth is defined as an absence of epithelial elements, with only stroma, in 1 low power field: typically 4x magnification). The tumor borders are well-defined and mitotic count is low (< 5 mitoses/10 high-power-fields [HPF]). On the other hand, malignant phyllodes tumors may display marked stromal cell atypia with increased cellularity, peripheral stromal condensation, and stromal overgrowth, as seen in this case. The mitotic count is usually beyond 10 mitoses/ 10 HPF and the tumor border may be diffusely permeative.

Biphasic metaplastic carcinoma often has an epithelial component harboring in situ or invasive carcinoma, which is a key clue in distinguishing between metaplastic carcinoma and malignant phyllodes tumor. In monophasic metaplastic carcinomas that lack epithelial components, immunohistochemistry for keratins may prove useful. However, a subset of phyllodes tumors may exhibit focal keratin, p63, and p40 positivity, which may be a diagnostic pitfall. Metaplastic carcinomas would usually be negative for CD34, while phyllodes tumors would be immunopositive for this antigen.

Fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma (F-LMC) is on the differential for a pink, fibrosing lesion and can mimic phyllodes tumor, but would lack marked atypia and giant stromal cells. F-LMC would also be cytokeratin positive. Of note, unlike desmoid fibromatosis (DF), F-LMC lacks nuclear beta-catenin expression.

The diagnosis of a metastatic sarcoma to the breast, which is an uncommon presentation, must be correlated with the clinical history of a prior sarcoma diagnosis; this patient did not have a history of a sarcoma at another site.

Of note, MED12 and RARA gene mutations are frequent in fibroepithelial lesions and are not seen in metaplastic carcinomas. These mutations are believed to be implicated in phyllodes tumorigenesis.

clinical.vignette: This is a 65-year-old female with an upper lip mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Canalicular adenoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a relatively well-circumscribed, encapsulated, basophilic neoplasm with monotonous low cuboidal to columnar cells arranged in evenly-spaced trabeculae and cords. There is densely eosinophilic and capillary rich stroma interlaced between the bilayered cords of cells. The nuclei are round and uniform, with no mitotic activity identified. The findings are consistent with the diagnosis of canalicular adenoma.

Discussion:

Canalicular adenoma is a single or multifocal benign cellular proliferation grossly characterized as a movable, well-delineated small nodule(s) that classically presents in the upper lip’s minor salivary glands in elderly females. It is extremely rare in the major salivary glands (i.e., parotid, submandibular glands). Canalicular adenoma is derived from the minor salivary gland terminal duct epithelium. The differential diagnostic considerations include tumors that also appear "blue" under low-power, including basal cell adenoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and pleomorphic adenoma with canalicular-like pattern among others.

Basal cell adenoma would be comprised of a majority of basaloid cells with some myoepithelial differentiation and more collagenous stroma. Immunohistochemical modalities that may assist in the diagnosis include beta catenin, which should be nuclear-stain positive in basal cell adenoma and not in canalicular adenoma.

Pleomorphic adenoma with canalicular-like pattern (PACL) would retain the triphasic features of pleomorphic adenoma (i.e., ductal, myoepithelial, and myxoid stromal cells), of which canalicular adenoma lacks the myxoid stromal component. In PACL, HMGA2-WIF1 gene fusions have been described.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) contains a dual population of ductal and myoepithelial cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and hyalinized stroma. This neoplasm would be invasive and exhibit a cribriform, solid, and/or tubular pattern. Most importantly, ACC lacks capillaries in its stroma.

clinical.vignette: This a 50-year-old male with a thyroid mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Differentiated high-grade papillary thyroid carcinoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a well-circumscribed, encapsulated, solid and sheet-like proliferation of atypical amphophilic cells, with nested and corded architecture as well as gland-like tubular structures. The nuclear features are striking for such a sheet-like neoplasm as the nuclei are grooved, contain clumped chromatin, and exhibit clearing, akin to papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclei. The high-grade architecture, in combination with the nuclear features, leads us to the diagnosis of differentiated high-grade papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Discussion:

Differentiated high-grade papillary thyroid carcinoma (DHGPTC) is a recent entity added to the 5th edition of the 2022 World Health Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours, and falls under the domain of differentiated high-grade thyroid carcinomas. Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common subtype of differentiated high grade carcinoma of the thyroid, followed by high-grade follicular and oncocytic thyroid carcinomas. The true incidence may be underestimated due to its rarity and recent recognition; it is most common in the elderly and in women.

The Turin criteria of classification of thyroid tumors defines poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PDTC), another high-grade member of the differential diagnosis, based on solid/trabecular/insular growth pattern, absence of conventional PTC nuclear features, and at least one of the following present: convoluted nuclei, mitotic activity >=3/10hpfs, or tumor necrosis. In our case, dominant solid, trabecular, and insular growth patterns combined with PTC nuclear features rules out a PDTC, and the Turin criteria classifies this case as more fitting of a DHGPTC. DHGPTC may have an equal, or even worse prognosis than PDTC because of the presence of radioactive iodine refractory (RAI) tissue present in high quantity in DHGPTC as compared to PDTC.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) may be considered given the nesting of the current lesion. It would stain for markers of neuroendocrine differentiation such as synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1 (insulinoma-associated protein 1), the last of which is a relatively new marker used in classifying neuroendocrine neoplasms. MTC may also be expected to contain fine, stippled, salt-and-pepper nuclear chromatin.

Parathyroid carcinoma may be differentiated from a thyroid malignancy based on preoperative radiograph/ultrasonographic assessment. In comparison to our case, parathyroid carcinoma would lack the nuclear features of PTC and be immunoreactive for parathyroid hormone, GATA3, and neuroendocrine markers while negative for thyroglobulin and PAX8.

clinical.vignette: This is a 30-year-old female with a nasal mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Sinonasal carcinoma with DEK-AFF2 gene fusion

answer.diagnosis: Sinonasal carcinoma with DEK-AFF2 gene fusion
answer.text:
Correct answer: Sinonasal carcinoma with DEK-AFF2 fusion

Histology:

Histologic sections demonstrate complex exophytic, endophytic, and confluent growth with broad papillary fronds and anastomosing lobules lined by hyperchromatic, thickened, non-keratinizing squamous epithelium with monotonous nuclei. Neutrophils are present in the surface epithelium and may cause confusion with sinonasal papilloma. This case demonstrated a DEK::AFF2 FISH break apart translocation, confirming the diagnosis of sinonasal carcinoma with DEK-AFF2 fusion.

Discussion:

Sinonasal carcinoma with DEK-AFF2 fusion is a recently described entity in the 5th edition of the 2022 World Health Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours, and falls under the family of non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinomas. It characteristically comprises broad papillary fronds with ribbons and nests of confluent growth and thickened, hyperchromatic non-keratinizing squamous epithelium. This diagnosis requires confirmation of a DEK::AFF2 break apart by fluorescent in-situ hybridization (FISH) analysis. In contrast to DEK-AFF2 carcinoma, a typical sinonasal papilloma (which is subdivided into three types: inverted, oncocytic, and exophytic) will not show this degree of confluent, back-to-back broad papillae and hyperchromatic nuclei. Both entities share a neutrophilic infiltrate with microabscesses in the surface epithelium as well as stark lack of keratinization.

SWI/SNF complex-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, also colloquially known as the SMARC-deficient tumors, typically do not show this confluent broad branching papillary pattern and instead are solid confluent sheets of small-to-medium sized monotonous basaloid cells with prominent nucleoli. The most common subtype is a SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma, and this subtype may occasionally form glands or have a yolk-sac like appearance with Schiller-Duval-like bodies.

HPV-associated multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma shares histologic and immunostaining features of salivary-type carcinomas and squamous cell carcinomas, with a biphasic population of cells undergoing ductal and myoepithelial differentiation with adenoid cystic carcinoma-like areas (cribriforming). Frequently, there is an associated squamous cell carcinoma in -situ along with squamous differentiation in the invasive tumor. Higher-grade features may include sarcomatoid and cartilaginous differentiation. Increased mitotic activity and necrosis are common.

clinical.vignette: This is a 60-year-old female who underwent lung wedge resection for a lung mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Cryptococcosis

Histology:

Histologic sections demonstrate unremarkable background lung parenchyma with a notable hypercellular nodule with areas of necrotic debris. On higher power, the areas of necrosis are separated by a dense lymphocytic infiltrate and cystic spaces; these cystic spaces contain tan grey spheroid bodies that would be India-ink stain positive on endobronchial laboratory examination and that are fungal organisms. These findings are indicative of cryptococcosis.

Discussion:

Cryptococcus is a genus of fungus (the two pathogenic subtypes are Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii), that naturally exists in bird droppings, rotting wood, and soil, and causes disease in humans when the spores are inhaled. It is frequently associated with human immunodeficiency virus infection (HIV), and Cryptococcus neoformans infection is in the category of AIDS-defining diseases. It may also present in those who are immunocompromised for other reasons other than AIDS, such as chemotherapy treatment or who have defects in cellular immunity. Of note, Cryptococcus gattii may affect immunocompetent individuals as well.

The organism presents as tan grey spherules occupying cystic spaces in a background of necrotizing inflammation in the lungs of immunocompromised patients. India-ink stain highlights Cryptococcus spp organisms as the stain cannot penetrate their gelatinous capsules, causing a halo effect around the fungi (known as a negative stain). In the modern era, detection of capsular material cryptococcal antigen by ELISA provides definitive diagnosis. Necrotizing inflammation/reaction to tissue injury is typical of Cryptococcus spp infection, and careful investigation of the necrotic component of a lesion is critical.

Fluconazole/amphotericin B or other antifungal agents, combined with treating the underlying immunodeficiency, are the main modalities of treatment.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (MTB) will present with necrotizing inflammation but they are not present here. MTB as well as other acid-fast bacilli are best highlighted on histology with an acid-fast bacilli stain that highlights them in red under 40x magnification. Careful investigation of multiple levels of the necrotic granuloma may be necessary in revealing the mycobacteria.

Metastatic adenocarcinoma may present with cellular necrosis, not just simply necrotic debris. Cellular necrosis is a form of necrosis where the cell outlines, termed “ghost cells”, are seen. In the context of carcinoma, cellular necrosis may occur due to tumor cells outstripping their blood supply and thus the center of the tumor begins to die. Instead of seeing ghost outlines of cells, necrotic debris and portions of cellular material are seen here. No atypical cells with large nuclei, hyperchromasia, nor atypical mitoses are present.

Sarcoidosis is an autoimmune disease that is characterized by the formation of non-necrotizing granulomas. These non-necrotizing granulomas may occur anywhere throughout the body; however, the brunt of the mortality is due to granuloma formation in the heart and lungs which may cause restrictive cardiomyopathy and restrictive lung disease/pulmonary fibrosis.

clinical.vignette: This is a 46-year-old female who underwent lung wedge resection for a lung mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Metastasizing leiomyoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of unremarkable background lung and a single, well-circumscribed and delineated, hypercellular nodule composed of long, sweeping fascicles of bland spindled smooth muscle cells that appear to entrap respiratory epithelium. Stark atypia is not present. The patient had a history of a leiomyoma that was treated with hysterectomy. Thus, given the history and the bland nature of this lesion, it is best regarded as a metastasizing leiomyoma.

Discussion:

Greater than 40% of retroperitoneal leiomyomas were reported in patients having concurrent uterine leiomyomas or who had underwent previous hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma, suggesting multifocal origin. Metastasizing leiomyoma results from hematogenous spread of uterine leiomyoma, most commonly to the lungs. A key to the diagnosis is two-fold: the history of a uterine leiomyoma or a hysterectomy for the same, and the low-power view of the lesion being a well-circumscribed nodule. Generally, metastases to the lung present as well-circumscribed, delineated masses, whereas primary pulmonary masses tend to be infiltrative and spiculated. Metastasizing leiomyomas are shown to be clonally related to a patient’s uterine leiomyoma, and they are hormonally sensitive; these commonly multifocal lesions may progress during pregnancy and regress during menopause.

The diagnosis of metastasizing leiomyoma must be made with proper rule-out of a metastatic leiomyosarcoma. Leiomyosarcoma would contain greater cytologic atypia, necrosis, and increased mitotic activity with atypical mitoses. If a patient had already underwent a hysterectomy for leiomyoma, it may also be helpful to obtain slides of the resection specimen for comparison.

Sclerosing pneumocytoma is distinctive, as it is one of the few benign primary lung neoplasms. It is characterized as a well-demarcated lesion with a biphasic population of cuboidal epithelium that resembles type II pneumocytes along with round stromal cells. Foamy macrophages may also be present, and tumor-associated alveolar hemorrhage may lead to hemosiderin deposition. It would lack the spindling and uniformity of the current case.

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis is a cystic, mesenchymal lung neoplasm arising from aberrant smooth muscle cells surrounding lymphatics. It can cause progressive parenchymal damage almost exclusively in premenopausal females, and is associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Histologically it is characterized by multiple thin walled cysts surrounded by nodules of spindled smooth muscle-appearing cells without frank cytologic atypia or mitoses, and hemosiderin laden macrophages may be present. This may hint to hemorrhage from cysts invading nearby vasculature.

clinical.vignette: This is a 37-year-old male with a splenic mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct diagnosis: Sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation (SANT)

Histology:

Histologic sections are comprised of confluent angiomatoid nodules surrounded by sclerotic stroma and a stark lack of white pulp. Upon closer examination, spindled endothelial cells and slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated red cells predominate. There is no frank cytologic atypia nor mitoses. The distinctive low power appearance of multiple angiomatoid, vascularized nodules is indicative of the diagnosis of sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation (SANT).

Discussion:

Sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation (SANT) is a rare benign, non-neoplastic splenic lesion (thus far, only described in the spleen) that is characterized by discrete to confluent vascularized nodules with spindled to plump endothelial cells, extravasated red cells, and slit-like vascular spaces in a collagenous, sclerotic stroma rich in fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. The pathogenesis is not completely understood. Surgical intervention is curative and recurrences have not been reported for this lesion.

Interestingly, three different vessel types within the nodules can be characterized by immunohistochemistry: capillaries (CD34/CD31-positive and CD8-negative), sinusoids (CD34-negative, and CD8/CD31-positive), and small veins (CD34/CD8-negative and CD31-positive). These are components of the red pulp and have been hypothesized as an exaggerated red pulp reaction to some stimulus. IgG4+ plasma cells may be numerous in this lesion but serum IgG4 is not elevated.

Littoral cell angioma is characterized by an enlarged spleen filled with multiple hemorrhagic, lobular nodules that are composed of pleomorphic, tortuous vascular spaces in the red pulp with papillary projections lined by plump endothelial cells. The splenic littoral cells that line the splenic red pulp sinuses have histiocytic and endothelial differentiation with positivity for CD68 and CD31, yet interestingly, lack CD34 positivity. Littoral cell angioma is associated with visceral malignancies such as colonic and pancreatic adenocarcinomas.

Angiosarcoma is characterized as an infiltrative lesion with atypical endothelial cells that may exhibit hobnailing, line vascular spaces, and may exhibit necrosis and increased mitotic activity; some variants may appear epithelioid and lack apparent vascular spaces. It would not present as a multinodular lesion such as in the current case.

Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma is a rare, borderline malignant mesenchymal tumor characterized by solid nodules of spindled or epithelioid cells, blood lakes and pseudoangiomatoid spaces, with a fibrous pseudocapsule and prominent peripheral lymphoplasmacytic cuff. It is commonly found in the superficial extremities, trunk, and head and neck. Despite the similarity of the name to our current lesion, there are no slit-like vascular spaces; instead there is a whorled pattern with histiocytoid morphology, and the lymphoid cuff and fibrous pseudocapsule distinguish this entity from SANT.

clinical.vignette: This is a 59-year-old male with a 22 cm right-sided retroperitoneal mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Inflammatory subtype of liposarcoma (inflammatory liposarcoma)

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a dense, sheet-like collagenous stroma embedded with cells containing hyperchromatic, atypical nuclei. A low power impression also reveals the presence of multiple lymphocytic aggregates along with a scant lymphoid infiltrate percolating through the dense collagenous stroma. Despite the bland appearance, the presence of lymphoid aggregates, large size (>20 cm), collagenous stroma, and retroperitoneal location are suggestive of inflammatory liposarcoma.

Of the three subtypes of well-differentiated liposarcoma (WDLS): lipoma-like, sclerosing, and inflammatory, inflammatory liposarcoma is the rarest subtype.

The lipoma-like subtype is the most common and predominantly composed of mature-appearing fat with scattered atypical, hyperchromatic cells of varying proportion. The sclerosing subtype is the second-most common form, commonly arising in the retroperitoneum and pelvis, and is predominantly composed of fibrous stroma with scattered bizarre hyperchromatic stromal cells, and multivacuolated lipoblasts. The fibrous component may encompass the majority of the lesion and may be difficult to distinguish from other non-lipogenic tumors. Inflammatory liposarcoma almost always arises in the retroperitoneum and is composed of lymphoid aggregates of varying proportions scattered in thick fibrocollagenous stroma with atypical, hyperchromatic cells that may also obscure adipocytes just like the sclerosing variant of WDLS. Clues to the diagnosis include the presence of lymphoid aggregates and a percolating lymphocytic infiltrate.

Fibromatosis, especially desmoid fibromatosis (DF), may occur in the intra-abdominal cavity and be confused with the inflammatory and sclerosing variants of liposarcoma. Clues to the diagnosis are the long, sweeping, and sometimes paucicellular fascicles of monomorphic fibroblasts with flattened, pencil-thin nuclei in DF, and absence of scattered atypical hyperchromatic cells. Lymphoid aggregates would be rare. Nuclear beta-catenin expression would be typical of DF.

Leiomyosarcoma would be characterized by having sweeping fascicles of neoplastic cells demonstrating smooth muscle differentiation with marked nuclear atypia, increased mitotic activity, and necrosis; myxoid areas and hyalinized stroma may be seen. The features seen in the current case are too bland, and the lymphoid aggregates would be atypical for, a high-grade lesion like leiomyosarcoma. Of note, there is a subtype known as inflammatory leiomyosarcoma that may share similar lymphoid aggregates with inflammatory liposarcoma. The presence of xanthomatous cells, fascicular pattern, and immunopositivity for SMA, desmin, and caldesmon may be useful for ruling in inflammatory leiomyosarcoma.
