clinical.vignette: This is a 19-year-old male with a spine mass. This is the resection from the posterior elements along with preoperative axial spinal computed-tomography radiograph. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Osteoblastoma

Radiographic and histologic description:

Axial CT demonstrates a well-circumscribed, well-delineated lytic mass in the left posterior vertebral arch/neural arch with speckled white areas of matrix mineralization. On histologic examination of the lesion elements, interconnected woven bone deposition by osteoblasts are embedded in vascularized fibroblastic stroma. The osteoblasts and associated osteoclasts lack significant atypia. Blood filled clefts reminiscent of aneurysmal bone cyst-like changes. The circumscription, speckled white areas, and location along the spine/posterior elements in an adult are indicative of an osteoblastoma.

Discussion:

Osteoblastoma is a locally aggressive neoplasm with similar histologic features to osteoid osteoma; in contrast to the latter, osteoblastoma has growth potential beyond >2 cm. Classic clinical scenarios may involve bone pain that is not relieved by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The posterior elements, especially the neural arch, are a characteristic location. IN contrast, osteoid osteoma in a radiographic impression predominantly affects the long bones, but the neural arch may rarely be affected; osteoid osteoma rarely exceeds >1 cm in maximal diameter. Osteoid osteoma is also characterized as containing a nidus, visible radiographically and histologically, as an area of pinpoint intensity with increased osteoblasts next to woven bone.

Conventional osteosarcoma would present with signs of aggressive behavior on radiographs such as expansile, lytic, and ill-defined borders. Codman’s triangle and sunburst pattern are radiographic examples of malignant periosteal reaction in response to osteosarcoma. Histologically there is neoplastic lace-like osteoid deposition with marked osteoblast atypia, frequent atypical mitoses, and necrosis.

Myositis ossificans, grouped with fibro-osseous pseudotumor of digits, is a neoplastic proliferation of osteoblasts that forms extraosseous bone. A history of antecedent trauma may be present. Radiographically and histologically, lesions often display a “zonation” pattern of ossification and mineralization. This is comprised of a hypercellular center with osteoblasts surrounded by woven bone, and maturation of lamellar bone at the periphery.

clinical.vignette: This is a 1-year-old male with a chest wall mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Maturing lipoblastoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a well-circumscribed, lobulated proliferation of maturing fat separated by fibrous septations. No fibrin thrombi, nor notable spindle cell proliferation with collagen is present. These histologic findings, especially occurring in a 1-year-old at the chest wall, are most consistent with a maturing lipoblastoma.

Discussion:

Lipoblastoma is a benign neoplasm of embryonal white fat, and can be diffuse (also known as lipoblastomatosis). It characteristically demonstrates lobulated architecture with maturing lipoblasts and adipocytes separated by fibrous septae in concert with peripheral myxoid mesenchymal elements. Myxoid areas are not seen here and demonstrate that this fat-containing neoplasm is maturing, hence the designation “maturing lipoblastoma”. It is not uncommon for a lipoblastoma to be biopsied as such and the resection to demonstrate a fibrolipomatous appearance without lipoblasts. Grossly, lipoblastomas commonly present on the trunk or extremities and are typically small but can exceed 10 cm with a soft, lobulated yellow-to-white appearance with myxoid, cystic, or fatty internal nodules. Lipoblastoma is commonly characterized by alterations of the PLAG1 gene on chromosome 8.

Lipomas are the main differential consideration and show overlap with the current case; however the age of the patient (infant) with presentation along the trunk is characteristic of a lipoblastoma. An angiolipoma would demonstrate more vascular components, and fibrin thrombi is a desirable histologic feature; both are not seen in this current case. Spindle cell lipoma/pleomorphic lipoma is characterized by fatty differentiation and variable amounts of bland spindle cells with ropy collagen bundles, which are not seen in the current case. Angiolipomas and spindle cell lipomas would be rare in an infant.

clinical.vignette: This is a 30 year old female with a placental nodule. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor

Histology:

Sections show proliferation of alternating hypocellular and hypercellular myofibroblastic cells with red blood cell extravasation, a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, and a myxoid background. There is prominent arcuating vasculature and vacuolated spindle cells with uniform chromatin and with areas exhibiting a myxoid appearance and architecture. Immunohistochemical stains performed demonstrate the following: ALK = negative, FISH analysis (fluorescent in situ hybridization) indicates no detectable rearrangement involving the ALK gene region. Despite lack of ALK gene rearrangement, the morphology is in keeping with an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. Since this tumor can locally recur or be locally destructive, close clinical follow-up is recommended.

The differential diagnosis includes chorangioma, leiomyoma, low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma, and other sarcomas with metastatic involvement of the placenta. In fact, involvement of the placenta by sarcoma has only rarely been reported.

choices: Endometrioid carcinoma with yolk sac tumor differentiation

answer.diagnosis: Endometrioid carcinoma with yolk sac tumor differentiation
answer.text:
Correct answer: Endometrioid carcinoma with yolk sac tumor differentiation

Histology and differential diagnosis discussion:

Sections show an ovarian well-differentiated endometrioid adenocarcinoma with extensive squamous differentiation (not shown) with adjacent high-grade component. This high-grade component exhibited reticular pattern in which a labyrinth of channels lined by primitive cells focally expand to form microcysts lined by clear or flattened, atypical epithelial cells. Focal differentiation into somatic endodermal gland-like structures are seen. The epithelial cells exhibit subnuclear and apical vacuoles resembling early secretory endometrium. Hyaline globules are conspicuous both within cells and in the stroma.

Immunohistochemically, this high-grade component shows: Pax8: negative; Sall4: positive (diffuse); AFP: positive; Glypican 3: positive; HNF-1b: focally positive; Napsin A: negative; ER: negative. The morphology and immunoprofile support a yolk sac tumor. Since this tumor is adjacent to an endometrioid tumor, this phenomenon either represents a collision event (somatic tumor/endometrioid carcinoma and germ cell tumor) or a somatic tumor (endometrioid carcinoma) with yolk sac tumor differentiation. We favor the latter.

For the yolk sac tumor, the main differential diagnoses include clear cell carcinoma, high-grade endometrioid carcinoma or serous carcinoma. The morphology and immunoprofile facilitate a definitive diagnosis.

clinical.vignette: This is a 60 year old female with a uterine mass and a lung lesion with similar morphology. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct diagnosis: Mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma

Histology:

Microscopic examination revealed a carcinoma with not only a predominant tubular architecture but also a variety of growth patterns, including focal solid growth with solid appearance, trabecular, glandular/pseudoendometrioid morphology. The tubules and glands were lined by nonstratified cuboidal and columnar cells with uniformly moderate cytologic atypia, variable eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm, and crowded nuclei with vesicular chromatin. Luminal eosinophilic material/secretion was present in some tubules. Immunohistochemical stains reveal: MLH1, MSH6, MSH2, PMS2, and intact expression of all 4 genes. ER/PR are negative. P53 displays normal/wild-type expression, p16 displays patchy expression. WT1 is negative, and PAX8 is positive. A TTF-1 is patchy positive and a GATA3 is focal and weakly positive.

Differential diagnosis discussion:

The differential diagnosis includes: endometrioid adenocarcinoma, mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma, serous carcinoma of endometrium, and clear-cell adenocarcinoma. PAX8 positivity, at its base, shows gynecologic origin. Wild-type p53 excludes serous carcinoma of endometrium. A negative ER/PR may make endometrioid adenocarcinoma less likely. The morphology of this tumor does not fit the morphology of clear cell adenocarcinoma, which commonly cytoplasmic clearing and hobnailing. A TTF-1 patchy positivity and a focal weak GATA3 positivity may facilitate the diagnosis of mesonephric-like adenocarcinoma. Some cases show luminal CD10 staining pattern. Unlike mesonephric carcinoma in the cervix originating from the mesonephric remnant, mesonephric-like carcinoma is thought be Mullerian origin.

clinical.vignette: This is a 46-year-old female with a 22 cm intra-abdominal tumor. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: EWSR1-NFATC2 fusion sarcoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a hypercellular, vaguely multinodular and well-circumscribed neoplasm mainly composed of small round blue cells. In certain areas these small round cells appear to be embedded in a myxohyaline to fibrohyaline matrix. These features are compatible with the diagnosis of EWSR1-NFATC2 fusion sarcoma. An EWSR1-NFATC2 fusion was detected in this tumor, confirming the diagnosis.

Discussion:

Ewing sarcoma is characterized by a gene fusion involving one member of the FET family of genes (usually EWSR1) and a member of the ETS family (classically, FLI1 although fusions with ERG may occur). There exists a broad category of round cell sarcomas with EWSR1 or FUS fusions that involve partners unrelated to the ETS gene family (ETS = “E26-transformation-specific” or “Erythroblast transformation specific” transcription factor). Hence, these round cell sarcomas usually involve EWSR1 or FUS that are fused with other gene partners.

Some examples may include EWSR1-NFATC2, EWSR1-PATZ1, and others. In our correct diagnosis, EWSR1-NFATC2, it commonly manifests as a painful, locally destructive bone lesion and on histology erodes and percolates through bone trabeculae. It may also, in our case, rarely present intraabdominally. The spindled to rounded tumor cells embedded in myxohyaline stroma is highly characteristic. Of note, EWSR1-PATZ1 fusion sarcoma is characterized by hypercellular proliferations of small to medium-sized tumor cells with fine granular chromatin and little myxohyaline stroma.

Distinguishing between Ewing sarcoma and a round cell sarcoma with other ETS fusions may be difficult; however, Ewing sarcoma classically contains a vaguely lobular pattern with small round cells and cleared-out cytoplasm, secondary to glycogen deposits. Ewing sarcoma may also demonstrate neuroectodermal differentiation in the form of pseudorosettes. CD99 staining is highly sensitive, and NKX2.2 staining is highly specific, for Ewing sarcoma.

CIC-rearranged sarcoma is a high-grade sarcoma involving a fusion between CIC and, most often, DUX4. These most commonly occur in the deep soft tissues and are histologically characterized by primitive round cells with mild nuclear pleomorphism arranged in a lobulated configuration separated by fibrous stroma. Focal areas may contain more hypercellular areas arranged in a storiform configuration. Consistent staining for WT1 and diffuse nuclear staining for ETV4 is essential. CD99 staining may be variable.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor (DSRCT) is characterized as a neoplasm of uncertain differentiation, and can be identified by infiltrative nests of small, round, monomorphic cells embedded in fibroblastic/myofibroblastic, desmoplastic stroma. It is noted to have a EWSR1-WT1 gene fusion in classic cases, and most commonly presents in the abdominal cavity. Interestingly, the serosal lining of body cavities, which commonly give rise to DSRCT, has high transient fetal expression of WT1, which may explain why a fusion sarcoma between WT1 and a gene partner may occur in the abdomen.

Lastly, BCOR-rearranged sarcomas are a group of primitive round cell sarcomas that demonstrate BCOR alterations, either with BCOR-related gene fusions (BCOR-CCNB3), or internal tandem duplications of BCOR. They are characterized histologically by solid sheets of monomorphic round cells, scant cytoplasm, and thin fibrous septae. Strong staining for BCOR or molecular confirmation of a BCOR genetic abnormality is essential for confirming the diagnosis.

clinical.vignette: This is a 15-year-old male with a 4.6 cm right knee mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Giant cell tumor of soft tissue
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor, localized type

answer.diagnosis: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor, localized type
answer.text:
Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of a well-circumscribed hypercellular mass with aggregates of giant cells visible at low power. On medium power these multinucleated giant cells, as well as a population of mononuclear cells and hemosiderin deposition are present. This lesion presented as a mass near the synovium of the patient’s knee. These three histologic features, combined with location along the knee’s synovium, are indicative of tenosynovial giant cell tumor, localized type.

Discussion:

Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), also known as "giant cell tumor of tendon sheath", is an entity comprising localized and diffuse type. The diffuse type was formerly known as “pigmented villonodular synovitis”. The localized type is characterized by a well-circumscribed composition of multinucleated giant cells, mononuclear cells, and areas of hemosiderin deposition. These mononuclear cells in localized type have been further characterized as small histiocyte-like cells and larger epithelioid cells.

The diffuse-type is infiltrative and grows in expansile sheets, with multinucleated giant cells being less common than in localized-type. Cleft-like, pseudosynovial or pseudoalveolar spaces lined with red blood cells are prevalent in the diffuse-type.

Malignant forms of TGCT may contain sheets of mononuclear cells and exhibit increased mitotic activity with atypical mitoses and enlarged, pleomorphic nuclei.

Giant cell tumor of soft tissue (GCT-ST) shares overlapping morphologic features with TGCT; however, GCT-ST also contains richly vascularized stroma with prevalent mitotic activity, metaplastic woven bone deposition, and aneurysmal bone-cyst like changes. Giant cell tumor of bone is a separate entity from GCT-ST and characteristically arises in the epiphysis of skeletally mature patients (this 15-year-old, barring metabolic bone abnormalities, is not expected to be skeletally mature). Deep fibrous histiocytoma, like TGCT, is well-circumscribed but would not be expected to contain multinucleated giant cells; rather, deep fibrous histiocytoma harbors a storiform, hypercellular architecture with hemangiopericytoma-like pattern.

clinical.vignette: This is a 48-year-old male with a 6.5 cm right thigh soft tissue mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are comprised of a multinodular, infiltrative, fibroblastic, eosinophilic cellular proliferation at low power. On medium power, linear cords of epithelioid cells with pale cytoplasm and round nuclei are abutted by hyalinized, sclerotic bands of wispy collagen. This histologic pattern is indicative of the diagnosis of sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma.

Discussion:

Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma (SEF) is a rare, superficial malignant fibroblastic neoplasm characterized by cords of epithelioid cells with pale cytoplasm and round nuclei. SEF shares overlapping genetic profiles with low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma (LGFS), and in the same tumor SEF may merge into areas of LGFMS that contain alternating zones and nodules of hyper- and hypocellularity with faint myxoid stroma. In some cases, diagnosis may be difficult if the sclerotic stroma is absent, but recognizing a population of monotonous cells with MUC4 overexpression, present in 80-90% of SEF cases, may be useful. SEF may also express EMA and SMA. In the differential with infiltrative carcinoma, keratins may help as they are negative in SEF.

Myxofibrosarcoma is an infiltrative and locally aggressive neoplasm that is characterized by myxoid stroma and incomplete fibrous septae on low power with pleomorphic nuclei. In the high-grade form stark hypercellularity and frank nuclear atypia may be present. Some of the highest grade areas may have a propensity to transition into undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma-like (UPS-like) areas.

Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT), in the classic form, is comprised of an aggregation of spindled myofibroblasts with myxoid stroma set against an inflammatory background with little, if any, sclerosis. More hypercellular forms demonstrate fascicular proliferations with admixed inflammatory cells. The hypocellular fibrous pattern of IMT is characterized by hyalinized collagenous stroma with scant spindled cells and associated lymphoplasmacytic inflammation. Although anaplastic lymphoma kinase-gene (ALK) has been characteristically associated with IMT, it has been shown that ~50% of IMT may be ALK-negative; highly sensitive ALK antibody clones may improve detection.

clinical.vignette: This is an 89-year-old female with a right groin mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct diagnosis: D. Pleomorphic liposarcoma.

Histologic description:

Histologic sections are composed of a pleomorphic and anaplastic population of large epithelioid cells, with prominent nucleoli and clumped chromatin, admixed with plump spindled cells and frequent atypical mitoses. An area of lipoblasts, with the lipid vacuoles indenting and scalloping the nucleus, is identified. The identification of lipoblasts, in combination with an undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma-like pattern (UPS-like), is indicative of pleomorphic liposarcoma.

Pleomorphic liposarcoma, in essence, comprises the morphology of an undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma but with lipoblasts, confirming an attempt by the tumor to differentiate into fat. It contains a complex karyotype and does not harbor MDM2 amplification unlike well-differentiated liposarcoma and dedifferentiated liposarcoma. Unlike this case, dedifferentiated liposarcoma would contain a well-differentiated component with an abrupt transition to a high-grade component with marked pleomorphism. Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma would likewise contain a UPS-like pattern yet harbors areas of skeletal muscle differentiation, including rhabdoid cells. It would be immunoreactive for MyoD1 and myogenin. Lastly, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor would be associated with a nerve and exhibit markers of neural crest differentiation and not fatty differentiation.

clinical.vignette: This is a 50-year-old female with a left atrial appendage tumor. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Intimal sarcoma with chondrosarcomatous elements.

Histologic description:

Histologic sections are characterized by large areas of geographic, cellular necrosis with prominent neoplastic cartilage. There are remnant viable tumor cells that exhibit peripheral condensation, located away from the areas of necrosis, that assume an undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma-like pattern (UPS-like). Together with the location of this tumor and the viable tumor morphology, these point to a diagnosis of intimal sarcoma with chondrosarcomatous elements.

Intimal sarcoma most commonly arises in patients in the fifth and sixth decades of life, with a slight female predominance and a predilection for the left heart, atrium, aorta, and pulmonary trunk. Clinical and radiographic correlation is essential in the workup of an intimal sarcoma, with patients presenting with widespread tumor emboli in the pulmonary vasculature/systemic circulation and a pedunculated mass in the heart or great vessels upon radiographic imaging. Morphologically, intimal sarcoma commonly displays a high-grade sarcoma pattern such as UPS-like or MFS-like (myxofibrosarcoma-like) pattern, often with areas of peripheral condensation and large areas of cellular necrosis. Heterologous elements may also be present, including osteosarcomatous, chondrosarcomatous and angiosarcomatous elements. The majority of cases of intimal sarcoma display immunoreactivity with MDM2/CDK4.

The nodules of neoplastic cartilage in an intimal sarcoma may be difficult to distinguish from a metastatic chondrosarcoma, although the distinctive location, necrosis, presence of atypical UPS-like spindle cells with peripheral condensation, and no evidence of bone primary make the diagnosis of intimal sarcoma more likely.

Angiosarcoma, especially more poorly differentiated and epithelioid forms, may mimic the UPS like pattern of intimal sarcoma, and should be considered when investigating a cardiac sarcoma. A careful search for vasoformative areas is critical, along with immunohistochemical investigation with ERG and CD31.

Atrial myxoma is a benign cardiac neoplasm characterized by myxoid stroma and mostly bland to spindled cells. Necrosis, cartilaginous formations, and peripheral condensation of atypical spindle cells would not be characteristic of an atrial myxoma.

Bode-Lesniewska B, Debiec-Rychter M, Tavora F. “Intimal Sarcoma”. Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours. WHO Classification of Tumours, 5th Edition. 2020. Pp. 315-317.

clinical.vignette: This is a 39-year-old male with an 8 cm kidney mass which was resected. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Correct answer: Synovial sarcoma.

Histologic description:

The histological section, on low-power view, is comprised of a hypercellular proliferation with vague multi-nodularity and areas of pushing growth into the background unremarkable renal parenchyma. On medium power, many of the cells assume a rounded, uniform cytology, and some cells display a rhabdoid morphology. The hypercellularity and rounded, uniform, monomorphic cell population point towards a diagnosis of synovial sarcoma.

Discussion:

Synovial sarcoma is a translocation sarcoma mediated by the SS X/1/2/4: SS18 t(X;18)(p11;q11) translocation. Translocation sarcomas generally demonstrate a uniform cytology and architecture; thus, a low to medium power assessment of this lesion is important in recognizing this attribute. Because of this uniformity, synovial sarcoma may look deceptively bland in certain cases. Synovial sarcoma may also exhibit a fibrosarcoma-like pattern (not well-seen here), and thus is on the differential for any lesion that exhibits "herringbone pattern" architecture, such as a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor. Poorly differentiated forms may assume a round-cell morphology and have scattered CD99 positivity akin to Ewing sarcoma. Despite its name, synovial sarcoma is not derived from synovium; it is characterized as a tumor of uncertain cellular differentiation. EMA shows more consistent staining than cytokeratins in synovial sarcoma, and TLE1 staining is sensitive, but not specific.

Epithelioid sarcoma (ES) is an aggressive malignancy divided into distal-type and proximal-type. The distal type commonly arises on acral sites with a pseudogranulomatous growth pattern, and can be mistaken for granuloma annulare in some challenging cases. The proximal type/large cell type mainly arises in proximal extremities and superficial truncal regions and consists of nests and sheets of large, epithelioid to rhabdoid cells with prominent nucleoli and foci of tumor necrosis. Immunohistochemically and molecularly it Is characterized by near-complete INI1/BAF47 (SMARCB1) loss. Peculiarly, both the distal-type and proximal-type forms of ES show epithelial marker immunoreactivity (low and high molecular weight keratin + EMA) and may also show CD34 expression. It is important to note that ERG expression is observed in ES and may cause confusion with tumors of endothelial differentiation.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma fall under the umbrella of the "small round blue cell tumor" family, and are individually discussed here.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor is characterized by isolated nests to solid configurations of small round blue cells infiltrating through fibroblast/myofibroblast-containing desmoplastic stroma, and most commonly arises in the intra-abdominal cavity. It is also characterized by an EWSR1-WT1 gene fusion. Immunopositivity for cytokeratin, WT1 (with an immunohistochemical antibody directed against C-terminus) and dot-like positivity for desmin are characteristic.

Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is characterized by a monomorphic population of primitive round cells that demonstrate skeletal muscle differentiation. It may assume the characteristic alveolar growth pattern with separation by fibrovascular septae, or may present in a sheetlike pattern. Some areas may show differentiating rhabdomyoblasts. It is characterized by either a PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 gene fusion in the majority of cases. Immunoreactivity for markers of skeletal muscle differentiation such as Myo D1 and myogenin is typical.

Suurmeijer AJH, Ladanyi M, Nielson TO. “Synovial Sarcoma”. Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours. WHO Classification of Tumours, 5th Edition. 2020. Pp. 290 - 293

choices: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK positive
Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (NOS)

answer.diagnosis: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK positive
answer.text:
Histology:

Sections demonstrate a sheet-like proliferation of semi-cohesive large anaplastic cells with crinkled nuclear contours, prominent nucleoli, clustering and rosette-formation around vasculature with associated hemophagocytosis. The neoplastic cells are positive for ALK+, CD30+, CD68+, CD163+, CD3+, CD4+, CD7+, and negative for CD20-, EBER ISH, and CD8-. CD5 demonstrates well-delineated tumor cell perivascular rosettes. Together, these point to the diagnosis of ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma.

Differential diagnosis:

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) can be understood as the T-cell equivalent of the aggressive B-cell neoplasm known as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The neoplastic cells in ALCL are activated mature cytotoxic T cells that display a CD4+ phenotype along with CD30 positivity. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma would also be CD15+ combined with CD30+ positivity and will not display ALK positivity, and may also express positivity for PAX5, thus delineating CHL as a B-cell neoplasm. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS usually has a CD4 predominance as seen with the current case and contains variable CD30 positivity; it is usually ALK negative. Just like ALK-positive ALCL, histiocytic sarcoma is positive for CD68 and CD163 but will not demonstrate immunoreactivity for ALK, CD30, nor CD3. CD4 may not be helpful as it also stains histiocytes.

Of note, there is the entity known as ALK negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma, which will be CD30+ but ALK negative.

clinical.vignette: This is a 50-year-old male with a nasal mass. Select the correct diagnosis. H&E: CD45: CD4: CD56: CK AE1/3: EBER-ISH:

answer.text:
Histology:

Sections demonstrate a high-grade, hypercellular infiltrative discohesive neoplasm permeating between sinonasal glands on low to mid magnification. On high magnification the cells are small and display moderate amounts of nuclear atypia and crinkled nuclear contours. A provided CD4, CD56, CD45 demonstrate a lymphocytic, NK/T cell phenotype in the lesional cells. An AE1/AE3 is negative in the lesional cells and highlights background sinonasal glands. An EBER-ISH is positive This supports the diagnosis of extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma.

Differential diagnosis:

Extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma is a high grade lymphocytic neoplasm that most preferentially arises in the nasal mucosa although has been reported in the adrenal glands and esophagus, and comprises 5-10% of lymphomas in China with a second relative predominance in Hispanic males in Western countries. The clinical history of a fungating, nasal mass may raise suspicion for Wegener’s granulomatosis, but in this case CD45 diffusely highlights a lymphocytic neoplasm. CD56 and CD4, markers of NK and helper T cell differentiation, are positive and aid in the diagnosis. EBER ISH is positive in almost 100% of cases and appears to be a driver in the pathogenesis. Angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma has a polymorphic morphology with prominent endothelial cells, expansion of follicular dendritic framework, and with expression of PD-1, CD10, BCL-6, CXCL13 or CCR5, although larger cells may be EBER ISH positive. An undifferentiated sinonasal carcinoma will not display the discohesive architecture seen here, and would be positive for AE1/AE3 although it is important to note that undifferentiated carcinomas may lose keratin expression commensurate with the degree of undifferentiation. It would not be floridly positive for CD45 like in the current case. Lastly, T-cell large granular leukemia is a leukemic neoplasm most commonly presenting with splenomegaly with bluish, azurophilic large granules in T cells. There is commonly a T-cell large granular lymphocyte (TLGL) staining pattern on flow cytometry and IHC; involving +CD5, +CD8, +CD57, granzyme B, and T-cell alpha-beta although rarely gamma-delta TLGL may exist.

answer.text:
Histology:

Sections demonstrate a sheet of mixed inflammatory infiltrate, with a striking presence of eosinophils as well as larger, binucleated "owl eye nuclei" with prominent nucleoli. A provided CD15 and CD30 stain highlight these large binucleated cells. The inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of CD3 positive T cells as well as CD20 positive B cells. Epstein-Barr encoded RNA in situ hybridization (EBER-ISH) is negative. These histologic and immunohistochemical findings support for the diagnosis of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

Differential diagnosis:

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm notable for the small presence of neoplastic cells with binucleation, prominent nucleoli, resembling "owl eye nuclei" which are believed to originate from the preapoptotic germinal center B-cell, and current belief is that the neoplastic cells, termed Reed-Sternberg cells (RS) circumvent apoptotic signals by differentiating into a subset of CD30+ post germinal memory B cells. The 4 variants of classical Hodgkin's lymphoma (CHL) are nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte rich, and lymphocyte depleted, of which nodular sclerosis is the most common and portends the best prognosis and lymphocyte depleted portends the worst prognosis; it is also the rarest variant of CHL.

Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, although known under the Hodgkin name, has a different immunohistochemical staining pattern and different morphology of the neoplastic cells. Like CHL, NLP HL is composed of a small proportion of neoplastic cells that appear like popcorn cells but are overall smaller and stain for CD20 and CD45 (unlike the neoplastic cells of CHL which stain for CD15 and CD30 with negative staining for CD20 and CD45.) Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma will have (on the hematopathology scale) large cells with atypical, sometimes bizarre nuclear atypia that may resemble a dedifferentiated carcinoma. These may stain for CD10, BCL6, and MUM1 depending on the site of origin (germinal center B cells versus activated B cells [GCB versus ABC]) according to the Hans classification. Lastly, anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is considered the T-cell equivalent of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and is split into two entities with anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) immunohistochemical positivity and those with ALK nonreactivity. ALCL is usually CD30 yet there have been reports of ALCL that can mimic nodular sclerosis CHL.

clinical.vignette: This is an adult female with an ampullary mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

choices: Gangliocytic paraganglioma with invasive moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma

answer.diagnosis: Gangliocytic paraganglioma with invasive moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma
answer.text:
Histologic description:

Histologic sections demonstrate a hypercellular, amphophilic neoplasm arising in the submucosa. There appears to be 4 cell types in this neoplasm. First, there is an amphophilic, nested to trabecular, epithelioid "Zellballen"-like tumor pattern with prominent yet delicate intervening vasculature, and the cells contain stippled chromatin in a neuroendocrine-type morphology. Secondly, there is an infiltrative, glandular component exhibiting dystrophic calcification that seems to merge with the amphophilic nested neoplasm. The third component is comprised of a spindle cell component between the nests of cells. Fourth, there is a prominent ganglion cell-like component. Together, these histologic findings point towards the diagnosis of gangliocytic paraganglioma with a component of moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

Differential diagnosis:

Gangliocytic paraganglioma (GP) almost exclusively arises in the duodenum or around the ampullary region, although may very rarely arise in extraintestinal sites. Unlike traditional paragangliomas/pheochromocytomas, they are usually nonfunctional and do not produce catecholamines. The prognosis of this lesion is good; approximately 7% of cases metastasize yet they may recur if not completely excised. Histologically the lesion is typically based in the submucosal region and is unencapsulated. It is known for its triphasic morphology, with epithelioid zellballen-like cells, spindle cells, and ganglion type cells, although they may be unequal in proportion and distribution. In this case, not only is there triphasic morphology in the gangliocytic paraganglioma but there is an incidental, invasive, moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma that appeared to arise in the same location as the GP.

GP must be differentiated from paraganglioma, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, and ganglioneuroma. Paraganglioma will demonstrate a nested, "zellballen" pattern similar to that seen in the epithelioid cells of GP, but may also demonstrate cytologic atypia and S100+ sustentacular supporting cells arranged around the epithelioid cells instead of having discrete islands in GP. It would not have the triphasic morphology seen with GP. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (WDNET) would contain a similar nested, trabecular organization as seen here but would lack the triphasic morphology, and pancreatic polypeptide with progesterone receptor (PR) immunostains have been shown in some studies to aid in distinguishing the two. Ganglioneuroma may be confused with GP especially if ganglion cells predominate. However, ganglioneuroma is rare in the ampullary region and thus a careful search for the epithelioid and spindle cell components is warranted, especially given GP’s predilection for the ampulla. Lastly, large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma would exhibit marked cytologic atypia, with frequent atypical mitoses and would not demonstrate the triphasic morphology of GP.

The moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma component is unrelated to the GP and infiltrates through the GP in an independent fashion (an example of collision tumor).

clinical.vignette: This is a 45-year-old female with a sphenoid mass. Select the correct diagnosis.

answer.text:
Histologic description:

Sections demonstrate a hypercellular, uniform, spindled to round cell neoplasm with relatively prominent staghorn vasculature, hyalinized vessels, and areas that appear separate from, but come close to, histologically unremarkable nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. There is no necrosis, increased mitotic activity, nor overt nuclear atypia. Pockets of extravasated red blood cells are seen. These histologic findings are consistent with the diagnosis of sinonasal glomangiopericytoma.

Differential diagnosis:

Sinonasal glomangiopericytoma is an uncommon, perivascular myoid tumor with cells that appear to blend together with indistinct cell borders and demonstrating minimal atypia, no necrosis and rare mitotic activity. They are usually arranged around large vessels ("staghorn" vessels), known as the hemangiopericytoma-like pattern that is not specific to this entity and can be seen in solitary fibrous tumor and other soft tissue neoplasms. Most notably, this epithelial proliferation seen in this tumor can be separated from the epithelial surface as seen here (known as the "grenz" zone). It is most known for a CTNNB1 mutation with mutational activation of beta catenin and also associated with cyclin D1 overexpression. The beta-catenin immunostain will highlight nearly all tumor cells in a nuclear and cytoplasmic fashion.

Glomus tumor is a pericytic-like neoplasm but is extremely rare in the sinonasal region, and is positive for smooth muscle actin but negative for beta-catenin nuclear staining. Lobular capillary hemangioma, formerly termed pyogenic granuloma, is a vascularized, lobulated neoplasm on low magnification with a granulation tissue like morphology usually with a feeder vessel. It would be negative for beta catenin. Finally, solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) may have a hemangiopericytoma-like pattern, but may also contain keloid like collagen and has thin-walled vasculature, in contrast to the thick-walled vasculature in sinonasal glomangiopericytoma. SFT will be positive for STAT6 and negative for beta catenin nuclear staining.

clinical.vignette: This is a 20-year-old male with a chest wall mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer.text:
Histology: On low magnification, sections demonstrate a lobulated, eosinophilic spindle cell neoplasm intersected by fibrous fascicles and displaying areas of hyper- and hypocellularity (Antoni A and B areas, respectively). The lesion primarily resides in the reticular dermis, and the papillary dermis and overlying epidermis are unremarkable. Palisaded nuclei and intervening areas with eosinophilic fibrils (Verocay bodies) are visible even at low power. Upon high magnification, spindled cells in an eosinophilic matrix are seen. The hyper-lobulated appearance, presence of Verocay bodies, and Antoni A and B areas support the diagnosis of plexiform schwannoma.

Differential diagnosis:

Plexiform schwannoma is a rare variant of schwannoma that is characterized by a multinodular growth pattern on gross examination and a plexiform pattern on histologic examination (i.e., resembling an intersecting nerve or vessel plexus). They are composed solely of Schwann cells and exhibit Antoni A and Antoni B areas along with Verocay bodies. They may also exhibit hyalinized vessels but these were not particularly prominent in our case. It is important to differentiate plexiform schwannoma from plexiform neurofibroma, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, and traumatic neuroma. Plexiform neurofibroma will present with not only Schwann cells but also perineurial cells, fibroblasts, and transitional cells, but like plexiform schwannoma will also have a multifascicular branching pattern (akin to a "bag of worms"). Plexiform neurofibroma would not simply contain neoplastic Schwann cells as seen here. Traumatic neuroma is a hyperplastic reparative nerve reaction after injury, most commonly status post trauma or surgical intervention and is comprised of reparative neurons with “kinked” nuclei. Finally, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) is a high-grade neoplasm that demonstrates a uniform spindle cell configuration with nuclear atypia, tumor necrosis, >10 mitoses per high power field, and, in some cases, a fibrosarcomatous pattern with rare heterologous elements. Those cases of MPNST with rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation are also referred to as Triton tumor.

clinical.vignette: This is a 30 year old male with a liver tumor.

answer.text:
Answer: B. Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma

Histologic Description: This is a big pink cell tumor that arises in a relatively normal, non-cirrhotic liver. The neoplastic cells have abundant oncocytic cytoplasm, and are arranged in nests and cords. The stroma surrounding these nests is characterized by thick, plywood-like collagen which is referred to as lamellar collagen. This morphology, combined with the young age of the patient, supports the diagnosis of fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma. The diagnosis is supported by the presence of DNAJB1:PRKACA gene fusion.

Differential Diagnosis: Cholangioblastic cholangiocarcinoma may also present as a liver tumor in a young patient, and shares the areas of follicular architecture seen in the current case. However, that neoplasm typically demonstrates a biphasic small cell/large cell morphology, and lacks the lamellar fibrosis of the current case. Cholangioblastic cholangiocarcinoma typically labels for biliary cytokeratins such as cytokeratin 7, and demonstrates diffuse immunoreactivity for inhibin. It harbors a characteristic NIPBL: NACC1 gene fusion. Small duct type intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma typically features clustered proliferations of malignant small glands located in the periphery of the liver away from the large central ducts. These neoplasms are characterized by IDH1/2 gene mutations, BRAF mutations, or FGFR2 gene fusions. The neoplasms label for biliary cytokeratins and not for hepatocellular markers. The characteristic features of absence of cirrhosis, young age, oncocytic cytology, lamellar fibrosis, and DNAJB1::PRKACA gene fusion distinguish fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma from hepatocellular carcinoma NOS.

clinical.vignette: This is a 68 year old female with a long history of bladder cancer of flat and papillary type who undergoes a cystectomy due to BCG resistance.

choices: Nested urothelial carcinoma invading lamina propria

answer.text:
Answer: C. Nephrogenic adenoma

Histologic Description: Elsewhere in this specimen, there was invasive urothelial carcinoma involving the lamina propria and flat urothelial carcinoma in situ. However, in the section provided, there is florid reactive epithelium along with areas of ulceration and lining composed of cuboidal cells. These cells form tubules in the lamia propria, some of which have colloid like material in their lumens. The cells line the surface of fibrovascular cores that project above the surface. The cells do not demonstrate significant mitotic activity or atypia. Some of the tubules are surrounded by hyaline basement membrane. These are the typical features of nephrogenic adenoma.

Differential Diagnosis: Papillary urothelial carcinoma would feature fibrovascular cores lined by cytologically malignant urothelium, which is multilayered and composed of elongated nuclei. Nested urothelial carcinoma would feature irregular nests of bland urothelium which can form small cysts mimicking the tubules of a nephrogenic adenoma. Nested urothelial carcinoma would be more infiltrative than a nephrogenic adenoma. Adenocarcinoma would demonstrate greater cytologic atypia than seen in the current specimen, as well as infiltrative growth.

Nephrogenic adenoma is typically associated with irritation in the bladder. The tubules of nephrogenic adenoma may permeate the prostate or the superficial muscularis propria of the bladder, increasing the potential for misdiagnosis as adenocarcinoma.
